data.title: Nova Scotia Bets on Microelectronics Integration, Not Chip Fabs
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Nova Scotia is unlikely to become the next great destination for wafer fabs. But its semiconductor and microelectronics opportunity may be more relevant to the region’s economy: assembling the right mix of sensing, processing, communications, power, photonics, AI, and packaging technologies to solve hard problems in the ocean, in defense, in healthcare, and in energy.

It’s an important distinction, Jean-François Bousquet, program director of Dalhousie University’s MINDI Hub, said in an interview with EE Times. The province’s strength is not necessarily inventing the next standalone semiconductor device but building highly integrated systems that must work reliably in remote, power-constrained, and unforgiving environments, he said.

“Semiconductors will scare people away if we talk about semiconductors, but if we talk about integration of microelectronic systems, I think there’s a strong capability of integrating into various domains, especially in ocean tech,” Bousquet said.

Integration, not just chips

Semiconductor ecosystems are frequently measured in fabs, process nodes, venture funding rounds, or the presence of global chipmakers.

Nova Scotia’s ecosystem is developing by starting with an operational problem to define applications: ocean observation, underwater robotics, sonar, fisheries, environmental monitoring, naval systems, medical technology, and renewable energy. The technology stack, which includes microelectronics, follows.

For an autonomous underwater vehicle operating below Arctic ice for months, that stack can be formidable. The vehicle must sense, communicate, navigate, classify events, process data locally, and conserve every possible joule of energy. It may need AI acceleration, FPGA-based processing, GPUs in some applications, MEMS devices, photonics, lasers, specialized communications, and advanced sensing. It also needs to fit inside a very small, rugged, waterproof package.

“We have to find innovative ways of integrating our microelectronics and make our autonomous vehicles smart enough to be able to go under the ice in the Arctic,” Bousquet said. “They have to communicate, they have to sense, and they have to know what’s around them.”

Nova Scotia’s microelectronics story is increasingly an edge computing story—and the edge can be underwater, far offshore, or embedded in a compact defense or environmental platform.

Bousquet’s group is working on a project involving autonomous underwater drones, as well as coordination between underwater and aerial systems for remote-area monitoring. Those are inherently dual-use capabilities. The same class of integrated electronics can support defense and surveillance requirements while also enabling scientific research, environmental monitoring, resource exploration, and climate-related observation.

“We developed sensors that will measure the biological, chemical, and geological content of water in the ocean,” Bousquet said.

Nova Scotia’s semiconductor and microelectronics development is driven by Atlantic Canada’s industrial geography. The province’s capital, Halifax, is home to a great deal of defense research, naval presence, defense primes and suppliers, universities, ocean-technology companies, and the Centre for Ocean Ventures & Entrepreneurship. The region’s proximity to the Atlantic, Arctic routes, fisheries, offshore resources, and shipbuilding is less a branding exercise than a set of practical engineering requirements.

At the local level, the MINDI Hub (short for Microelectronics Innovation Design Hub) is meant to provide some connective tissue. Backed by the provincial government, the initiative is designed to support industry, develop curriculum around microelectronics for ocean technology, train students, and expand the workforce available to local companies.

MINDI is part of a wider Canadian tapestry. It is hosted at Dalhousie University, which collaborates with Quebec-based experts, including those at the University of Sherbrooke and Zero Point Cryogenics, while exploring international partnerships. Rather than duplicate every capability locally, the goal is to link Nova Scotia’s systems-level strengths to the specialized facilities, research talent, and suppliers available elsewhere in Canada and among allied countries.

“This is an incubator that’s intending to support industry, and we’re training students,” Bousquet said. “We’re building new curriculum around microelectronics for ocean technology. We want to create more momentum, and we want to create a bigger workforce that will actually support the local industry.”

Low-power innovation beneath the surface

Bedford-based Innovasea is a concrete example of how Bousquet’s regional thesis works in practice.

The company designs and manufactures aquatic technology, including acoustic telemetry systems used to track fish in oceans, lakes, and rivers. Its products are used by scientists and biologists studying animal movement and behavior, but the engineering behind them is broadly recognizable to anyone working in ultra-low-power embedded electronics.

Innovasea’s small acoustic tags attach to (or, in some cases, are implanted in) fish. Underwater receivers detect the transmitted acoustic signals, allowing researchers to identify tagged animals and, using multiple receivers, determine their locations with fine precision. The tag can also carry sensor data, such as temperature or pressure.

Jean Quirion, VP of R&D for fish tracking at Innovasea, told EE Times in an interview that the company’s competitive advantage lies in integrating components into compact, power-efficient systems that operate reliably in demanding environments.

He said increasingly efficient microcontrollers let designers perform more computation within an existing power budget or maintain performance while consuming less energy.

But these component improvements are not the only factors contributing to Innovasea’s engineering gains, Quirion said. “Most of the innovations that we’ve come up with that really reduce power consumption and reduce size have been in some tricks that we’ve developed internally to just make the system behave in a more power-efficient way.”

The expertise developed at Innovasea is due in part to connections between industry and universities. Quirion described Dalhousie as both a source of engineering talent, through co-op placements and full-time hiring, and a partner for research that carries more uncertainty than routine product development.

Collaboration with Dalhousie and other regional universities helps companies explore emerging technologies. Alongside organizations such as COVE, those relationships connect research, workforce development, and commercial engineering, supporting an Atlantic Canadian ecosystem whose opportunity lies in turning semiconductor capabilities into useful, exportable systems.

Building a connected ecosystem

Chris Morrissey, CEO of Invest Nova Scotia, sees microelectronics as an enabling layer within a wider economic strategy rather than a standalone vertical. The province has identified six priority sectors, including energy, defense, natural resources, AI, and the digital economy. Semiconductor and embedded systems capabilities intersect with all of them.

That is particularly evident in defense. Nova Scotia has naval and Coast Guard activity, shipbuilding, aerospace and drone-related capabilities, defense primes, and a growing supplier base. Morrissey said the province has between four and six major defense prime contractors and more than 100 defense companies, creating both procurement opportunities and demand for locally relevant R&D.

“The advantage that Nova Scotia has is the research and development expertise that we have here, both in the public and private sectors,” Morrissey said, citing MINDI as a good example of public funding.

Opportunities are not limited to military contracts, he said. Sonar and tracking technologies can apply to naval requirements and fisheries; drones can serve defense missions and support wildfire management; and sensing systems can contribute to environmental monitoring, energy operations, and safety.

Dual-use technology is a recurring theme in Nova Scotia, with companies able to extend a core competence into adjacent markets.

Within Atlantic Canada, Morrissey argued that provinces should identify complementary strengths rather than chase identical projects. Newfoundland and Labrador’s Marine Institute, for example, has capabilities in marine simulation and related areas. Nova Scotia can develop where it has distinct advantages in ocean technology, digital systems, defense, research, and talent. Morrissey said sustainable growth must align with available talent, capital, and infrastructure rather than build around a speculative attempt to replicate Silicon Valley.

“We can be complementary to each other,” he said. “We’re trying to find each of our own lanes and what’s the competitive advantage for each one but also working together and leaning on each other to make sure we can take advantage of the greater opportunity.”

That cooperative stance increasingly extends across the country. Bousquet’s quantum sensing work depends on Quebec partnerships; companies in Atlantic Canada can access expertise and markets nationally; and defense, ocean technology, photonics, and AI systems all depend on supply chains that exceed provincial borders. Internationally, Nova Scotia’s ocean-facing industries have natural links to Europe, NATO allies, and global marine research communities.

Bousquet said Nova Scotia does not need to reproduce another region’s semiconductor cluster to matter. It can build technologies that fit the problems in front of it and connect those systems to capabilities across Atlantic Canada, the country, and the world.

“We do have a lot of the capability; it’s just a matter of growing it,” he said.

At this year’s electronica, there was a clear emphasis on taking a system- and platform-level approach to enabling physical AI and edge AI. All the key chipmakers were talking about hardware-software platforms that help developers quickly build drones, physical AI and humanoid robotics systems, and use agentic AI to deliver edge AI systems.

We hear firsthand from our editors on the ground at electronica 2026 in Munich, Germany, in these two short videos.

Embedded and edge AI: Agentic tools, NPUs everywhere, and robot hands

Agentic AI is changing embedded development tool flows. Microcontroller makers, along with a growing number of smaller startups, are building AI agents for code generation and other design tasks. EE Times’ Sally Ward-Foxton notes that almost every microcontroller now has a dedicated NPU, and that companies such as Nordic Semiconductor want to be solution providers, not just silicon suppliers. We also talk about Europe’s strength in MCU design, why chipmakers are moving into software and subsystems, and the many robotic hand designs on show.

Power electronics: The AI data center dominates

Aaliya Shaukat, editor-in-chief of PowerElectronicsNews.com, talks about the show’s power side, which centered on the AI data center. Topics include solid-state circuit breakers and transformers, vertical power delivery, and recent deals such as Analog Devices’ acquisition of Empower Semiconductor. We also look at how wide-bandgap supply is being squeezed by data center demand, with Wolfspeed moving into GaN and Infineon scaling GaN on 300-mm wafers. Looking ahead, she expects data centers to remain the top story, with physical AI and humanoid robotics coming next.

data.title: Jensen Resigns Over Second Affair
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

A lot can change in a week. Just days after admitting to an extramarital affair with a Chinese intelligence asset, Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia CEO after The New York Times exposed a second affair with a senior Nvidia staff member.

As late as Wednesday evening, it looked like Jensen was going to ride out the scandal over his affair with the executive revealed to be a Chinese spy. But the emergence of a second affair, this time with one of Huang’s direct reports within Nvidia, was another huge blow. It was the coincident timing of these two separate scandals that really made Huang’s position untenable; he might have survived either one had they presented separately (then-Intel CEO Brian Krzanich resigned in 2018 over a similar offense, but he didn’t have Jensen’s history with the company, nor his star power).

The personal and professional reputation of the industry’s most famous CEO is now indelibly stained.

Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has been the CEO since day 1. In those 33 years, Nvidia has become the biggest tech company in the world, today worth around $4 trillion, largely due to the AI revolution. Nvidia GPUs became the de facto standard for machine intelligence and have driven almost all significant breakthroughs in AI in the last 10 years. During that time, Jensen managed Nvidia with a famously small team of around 42,000 (Intel has double that) in a unique style. The company executed ruthlessly and relentlessly under his leadership to become one of the most important companies in the U.S. economy today.

For his tenure to end like this is ridiculous; too far-fetched even for an episode of the HBO series Silicon Valley.

Jensen’s personal brand—the rockstar tech guru and charismatic business genius at the helm of the world’s biggest semiconductor company—is so irrevocably linked with Nvidia’s brand that it is going to be incredibly hard to separate them. But that is what must be done, and then, a new CEO must be found. For a company that has only ever had one CEO and with no obvious internal successor, that is going to be an enormous task. Nvidia’s board said it is considering internal and external candidates.

Even in the last few years, Jensen personally has had a huge impact on the industry with his bombastic stage presence and outspoken support for causes such as open-source models. He’s also given us so many iconic moments, from unveiling the A100 from the oven in his kitchen to introducing “Jensen math” and “the more you buy, the more you save.”

His departure has certainly left a big leather jacket to fill.

data.title: Can Machines See a Sick Plant Before a Farmer Can?
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Twelve days after planting soybean seeds in a greenhouse at North Dakota State University, researchers could distinguish plants affected by sudden-death syndrome from healthy plants using hyperspectral imaging. To the human eye, the plants still looked alike.

For Xin “Rex” Sun, director of the Peltier Institute for Advancement in Agricultural Technology at North Dakota State University, the experiment illustrates the promise of detecting crop disease before visible symptoms appear. His team said it identified spectral differences several days to approximately a week before they became visible.

The research has not yet been validated under field conditions. But it points toward a potentially valuable agricultural tool: a sensor that could identify problems early enough for farmers to intervene before damage becomes widespread.

The obstacle is economics. Hyperspectral cameras can cost tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars, require specialized expertise, and generate enormous quantities of data. Few farmers can justify that investment without a clear financial return.

Sun believes the solution may be to use hyperspectral imaging to discover which wavelengths reveal a particular disease, then build cheaper cameras that capture only those wavelengths.

Finding the wavelengths that matter

Conventional cameras capture reflected light in three broad bands: red, green, and blue. Hyperspectral imaging divides light into many narrower wavelength bands, revealing changes in a plant’s physiological or chemical condition that may not yet affect its appearance.

Sun’s laboratory recently acquired a short-wave infrared (SWIR) camera covering approximately 1,000 to 2,500 nm, with more than 200 spectral bands. Such equipment is valuable for research because scientists do not necessarily know which wavelengths will reveal the differences they are looking for. A farmer diagnosing one particular disease may need only a fraction of that information.

“That’s the beauty of using hyperspectral imaging technology,” Sun said. “It’s all about selecting the bands.”

He described a hypothetical case in which researchers discover that two or three wavelengths reliably distinguish soybeans affected by sudden-death syndrome from healthy plants. A multispectral camera capturing those wavelengths could then replace the much more expensive research instrument.

Sun’s laboratory already works with multispectral cameras containing four to 10 bands. Such devices can cost hundreds or thousands of dollars rather than the six-figure prices associated with some research-grade hyperspectral systems.

Reducing the number of bands also reduces the computing burden. Extensive hyperspectral measurements can generate hundreds of gigabytes or more of data, requiring substantial processing resources.

“If we can find three or four bands out of the hyperspectral imaging, those small processors can process them,” Sun said. “Then it can be fast enough in the field to give you a good result.”

But identifying useful wavelengths is only part of the challenge. Sun cautioned that disease and other stresses can produce similar spectral changes, particularly before symptoms become visible. Changing sunlight, soil conditions, and other environmental factors also affect measurements.

His team has been collecting agricultural imagery under different conditions to develop models that work outside controlled experiments. It has not yet established a sufficiently validated set of wavelengths for field diagnosis of soybean sudden-death syndrome.

Making spectral cameras like semiconductor chips

At Belgian semiconductor research organization imec, researchers are developing technologies that could make application-specific spectral sensors commercially practical. Carolina Blanch, a senior researcher working on hyperspectral imaging applications, agreed that many applications do not require the full spectrum.

“We typically start with high-resolution spectral cameras that capture around 100 bands, then identify which ones are most relevant,” she said. “For most applications, 10 or fewer bands are sufficient.”

However, designing a different sensor for every crop disease is not necessarily economical. Blanch said imec also develops standardized sensors with nine, 16, or 25 spectral bands, potentially serving multiple applications and spreading manufacturing costs across larger markets.

Klaas Tack, technical lead of hyperspectral imaging at imec, explained how semiconductor manufacturing could reduce costs further.

Traditional hyperspectral cameras often rely on separate optical components to divide incoming light into different wavelengths. Imec instead integrates spectral filters directly with image detectors during semiconductor fabrication.

“We developed a process in our fab where we integrate the filters with the detector,” Tack said. “Because we’re doing this at wafer level, we’re manufacturing many detectors at the same time.”

The approach reduces components, size, weight, and alignment requirements. It also enables compact snapshot sensors that capture spatial and spectral information in a single exposure, avoiding some motion artifacts associated with scanning cameras. That matters when sensors operate on moving tractors or drones, or when wind moves leaves during image acquisition.

Manufacturing volume is the remaining economic hurdle. Semiconductor fabrication involves substantial upfront costs, but producing large numbers of sensors could reduce their unit price dramatically.

Tack points to imec spinoff Spectricity, which targets smartphone applications with low-cost snapshot multispectral sensors. Those devices are not designed for agricultural disease detection, but they illustrate the potential economics of high-volume production.

“When the volume is high enough, you can dramatically reduce the cost,” Tack said.

From research instrument to farm equipment

Not every agricultural application will benefit equally from cheaper, silicon-based sensors. Some diseases and stress can be detected using visible and near-infrared wavelengths. Others benefit from SWIR measurements, which can reveal additional information about plant chemistry and water-related stress.

SWIR detectors remain more expensive than conventional CMOS sensors, and Tack said integrating spectral filters with them is more complicated. Further manufacturing advances may be needed to achieve comparable cost reductions.

For Sun, another challenge is converting spectral measurements into reliable decisions. His team is developing a field-based platform that could carry sensors through crops, diagnose problems, and eventually support interventions. The goal is to replace expensive laboratory analysis with affordable sensing and processing on agricultural machinery.

Tack believes the underlying visible and near-infrared sensor technology is already available for application developers, although he cannot predict when agricultural products will reach widespread deployment. “I think today we can provide them with the technology that is required,” he said.

Sun said he expects significant progress over the next five or six years but emphasizes that field validation remains essential. “If you’re a farmer, you need to think twice,” he said of investing in an expensive hyperspectral system. “If I spend that much money, I want to know how soon I get my money back.”

The potential benefit is not simply higher yields. Earlier and more accurate information could help farmers target interventions, avoid unnecessary treatments, and maintain production at a lower cost.

Hyperspectral imaging has already demonstrated that it can reveal differences invisible to the human eye. Making that capability useful on farms may depend less on capturing hundreds of wavelengths than on identifying the few that matter—and manufacturing sensors that farmers can afford.

data.title: Harari Warns Tech Leaders Against Pursuing AI Superintelligence
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

BARCELONA, Spain — Addressing corporate technology executives at the Gartner IT Symposium/Xpo, historian and philosopher Yuval Noah Harari warned that the tech industry’s race to create artificial superintelligence is a historic market failure driven by ideological fantasy rather than economic rationality.

In an onstage conversation with John Thornhill, editor of The Financial Times, Harari argued that treating autonomous software as a mere tool fatally misjudges its nature.

Urging CIOs and policymakers to halt the pursuit of uncontrollable digital gods, he called for redirecting capital and research away from general superintelligence and toward narrow, verifiable systems that address tangible problems.

Emergence of the digital agents

When asked whether AI represents a rupture comparable to fire, the printing press, electricity, or computing, Harari pointed to agents: “AI is the first technology which is an agent,” he said. While the use of fire and nuclear power depends on human intent, artificial intelligence acts independently. “It’s your decision whether to use fire to cook your meal or to burn a forest. It’s not a fire’s decision. AI is different because it can make decisions on its own. It can invent new ideas on its own. It can invent the next technology on its own. The printing press could not invent the radio. AI can invent better AI.”

Viewing AI systems as tools is an error: “It’s better to think about them as animals, or creatures, or aliens to really understand. This is not something in our hands. This is something in our relationship with us,” Harari said. When Thornhill asked whether autonomous agents could remain subservient, he replied: “Not if they are far more intelligent than us.”

That dynamic exposes an unresolvable commercial fallacy. “The first question: Will it be far more intelligent than us? And the industry bets it will,” Harari said. “The second question is: Do you know how to keep far more intelligent entities under your control? And the answer is obviously no,” and added: “If you create gods with the assumption that they will be your slaves and you can use them to do what you want, you don’t understand what gods mean.”

Addressing researchers who view superintelligence as an evolutionary upgrade, Harari separated intelligence from consciousness: “There is zero love and zero beauty, also zero pain and zero sadness,” he said. “It’s a completely dark universe, and there is no value in that kind of civilization.”

AI is a bureaucratic native

Turning to societal consequences, Harari argued that AI targets civilization’s bureaucratic operating system: “Bureaucracy is the underappreciated hero of history,” he said, noting that institutions generate trust through language. Software has now entered that realm: “AIs are bureaucratic natives. For us, bureaucracy is alien, strange, or foreign because we are millions of years older than it. We were born in the forest, and bureaucracy came along late in human evolution,” he said. “AIs are bureaucratic natives. They’re all born in the office, not in the forest, and they’re poised to take over all the bureaucratic systems of the world, from finance to religion.”

Rather than an accident, Harari identified human displacement as the primary danger: “Everything goes right, and the AI simply creates a new world which is way beyond the human ability to understand. Humanity will face a situation of collective dementia. Once upon a time, you were the most intelligent, capable, powerful agent around, and you understood and controlled everything in your own life, and then things changed, and you’re left behind.”

Harari expressed disbelief that markets are bankrolling their own demise: “The market is supposed to be rational. Nobody can calculate what would be the return on investment on creating gods.” Pointing to Elon Musk’s prediction that money could vanish within a decade, and prospectuses admitting existential risk, Harari characterized the race as an ideological crusade rather than a rational business enterprise.

Dumb refrigerators  and European sovereignty

Addressing immediate dilemmas facing corporate executives and citizens, Harari cautioned against fragile complexity: “Stupid refrigerators are much better than smart refrigerators,” he said, referring to recent hacks on supermarket fridges. “It’s like a chain with a hundred links. If just one link is not secure, everything crashes.”

When integrating software agents into operations, Harari advised executives to think sociologically: “We cannot think about them as tools. We need to think about them as agents, as entities. We are bringing new kinds of immigrants into our societies—not human immigrants, but digital immigrants. They are likely to have their own goals, their own way of doing things, increasingly their own tribes, their own networks of cooperation.”

For Europe, technological dependency represents a loss of sovereignty: “If you are a citizen of a country whose entire infrastructure, from hospitals and airports to the army, is based on AI technology that comes from across the ocean and that can be shut down at the press of a button, you are no longer sovereign,” Harari said. 

He outlined three strategic paths: accept vassal status to the U.S. or China; build independent national systems costing over €500 billion (~$554 billion); or establish shared European infrastructure through deeper federalization.

He said that the third option would be the best, but he warned that “Option number one is the trajectory in which Europe is going at present. And if you look at the issues that dominate politics in countries such as Spain, Germany, and the U.K., it’s clear that this is at present the direction,” he said, arguing that, being more preoccupied with human migration, Europe is sleepwalking into vassalage by ignoring digital immigration.

Call for limited AI and human collaboration

In his final recommendations, Harari urged CIOs to reject general superintelligence and focus on bounded applications: “I’m not talking about stopping all research in AI. It’s just directing it in other directions,” he said. “First of all, invest far more in safety, and secondly, don’t race to superintelligence. Focus on creating limited intelligence and deploying it here and now for beneficial results, whether in healthcare, transport, or ecology.”

Harari highlighted a psychological paradox: Developers justify racing ahead because they distrust human rivals, yet trust alien software. “With humans, at least we have thousands of years of experience. We know they can manipulate and cheat, and lie, but we also have substantial experience in how to overcome this and create robust systems of cooperation,” Harari said. “AIs already know that they can cheat and manipulate and lie, and we have almost no experience with how to build large-scale, robust systems of cooperation.”

Because complex general systems cannot be evaluated in a laboratory before deployment, Harari concluded that deliberate restraint is humanity’s most urgent safeguard.

In conclusion, Harari reiterated the need to buy time to ensure technology serves human welfare. In navigating that future, Harari maintained that preserving human agency is not an abstract ideal, but the essential condition for survival.

At electronica 2026 in Munich, EE Times talks with Lars Reger, CTO of NXP Semiconductors, about the physical AI era and how it reaches far beyond humanoid robots.

Lars introduces NXP’s new NavQ95 platform, built on the i.MX 95. It comes with reference designs, complete drone kits and robotics SDKs, so startups and newcomers can go from unboxing to a working robot or drone in about 30 minutes. He explains why most of the 50 billion smart connected devices expected by 2040 will be purpose-built machines rather than humanoids. Or, as he puts it, he won’t buy a humanoid to push his lawnmower.

The conversation also covers:

  • Why trust, security and functional safety matter in autonomous devices, from neonatal baby monitors to drones that can’t simply stop and reboot mid-flight.
  • Lars’s long-running “fridge hacking” warning, and why it’s now coming true.
  • How geopolitics is shaping NXP’s strategy: local-for-local security certifications, sourcing from two fabs on two continents, and RISC-V as an alternative architecture.
  • Why AI at the edge will arrive gradually as people replace old appliances, not as the step change Wall Street expects.

data.title: Dukosi Samples Contactless Battery Communication System for EVs, Grid Storage
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

BUDAPEST, Hungary – At the Pretzl Connect 2026 press event, Edinburgh-based Dukosi announced it has begun commercial sampling of its DK-NFLNK, a contactless intra-battery communication solution designed to eliminate wiring harnesses and improve battery safety.

By transmitting voltage and temperature data wirelessly across a single bus antenna via near-field RF rather than copper cabling, the system removes failure points from the battery architecture, contributes to real-time thermal monitoring using data collected from Dukosi’s DKCMS chips, and supports data tracking helpful for the battery passport.

The Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 of the European Parliament and of the Council mandates that “From 18 February 2027 each LMT battery, each industrial battery with a capacity greater than 2 kWh, and each electric vehicle battery placed on the market or put into service shall have an electronic record (‘battery passport’).”

Vulnerability of physical cabling

“Connector failure rates in a conventional wiring harness are around 10 parts per million,” said Joseph Notaro, president of Dukosi in Budapest. “In the automotive and industrial arenas where you’re looking at parts-per-billion-level reliability, that failure rate is simply too high and an unacceptable risk of failure.”

Wired networks also risk galvanic coupling between high-voltage circuits and low-voltage controls, plus added labor and weight. “With contactless technology, we decouple the high-voltage circuits and get rid of the physical connectors, which makes the system safer, higher quality, and more reliable over its entire operating life,” Notaro said.

Synchronous sensing at cell level

At the heart of Dukosi’s architecture is C-SynQ, a protocol that uses near-field radio signals along a single bus antenna wire. The signals operate at the cell level and stay within the enclosure, providing noise immunity without the need for line of sight.

“Smarter battery management starts with better data, and better data starts at the individual cell,” Notaro said. “When you’re deciding available power or charge limits, you want every cell being measured at the same time under the same conditions. That’s the technical equivalent of taking a high-speed photo of every cell at the same time.”

Notaro continued, “The weakest cell dictates the state of charge and the overall performance of the pack. If you don’t measure the cells in synchronization, then measurement errors creep in, and you’re forced to add in design margins, which in turn limit performance.”

Early warning for thermal safety

Li-ion battery safety is all about preventing thermal runaway. A short circuit in one cell can trigger an exothermic reaction that then spreads to adjacent cells. Older pack designs had only two or three temperature sensors across the whole module, so they didn’t monitor individual cells.

“In the traditional layouts with very sparse temperature sensing, the heat from a failing cell can take 10 to 15 minutes to get to an external sensor,” Notaro said. “With sensing capability on every cell, temperature excursions are detected almost immediately, well before the heat has a chance to propagate to the adjacent cells.”

Cell-level monitoring lets the software run outlier-detection algorithms by comparing the thermal profiles of the various cells and flagging minor deviations before they become a problem.

“Some manufacturers try to cut costs by getting rid of the sensors and just assuming the cells are all the same,” Notaro said. “Every chemical manufacturing process has variation. You can’t have a battery pack that’s that uniform and then ignore the cell-level monitoring without increasing your operating risk.”

During the briefing, EE Times asked whether battery manufacturers in China take a different approach to monitoring and safety compared to companies in other regions, specifically questioning if their strategies are primarily cost-driven. 

Notaro responded that China actually has two distinct tiers of customers: One that prioritizes safety and total system value, and another strictly focused on short-term component costs. He emphasized that this split is not unique to China, as carmakers globally divide between safety-conscious and cost-driven mindsets. 

He added that the massive volume of EVs in China provides domestic manufacturers with extensive operational data, accelerating their ability to refine battery quality over time.

Usable energy and lifetime traceability

Measurement precision directly affects usable energy capacity. The Dukosi Cell Monitoring System (DKCMS), built around the DK8102 Cell Monitor chip and DK8202 System Hub, directly addresses the system measurement errors that traditionally degrade usable battery capacity. “By providing consistent cell-level data, operators can reduce safety buffers and increase usable energy by 6% to 12%,” Notaro said. “You are not altering cell chemistry or adding weight; you are simply extracting energy previously locked away by measurement margins.”

For utility-scale energy storage, that efficiency gain has a direct financial impact. In a 200-MW installation, you can generate $8 million in additional revenue from the extra capacity or reduce capex by $2 million by needing fewer cells.

Dukosi’s monitoring technology could also support the collection of operational data relevant to the EU Battery Passport. From Feb. 18, 2027, batteries covered by the EU Batteries Regulation will require an electronic record containing information about their identification, composition, performance, and health. DKCMS chips incorporate onboard non-volatile memory and a unique silicon identifier attached to each cell.

“Every cell has its own digital passport on chip, which records the maximum temperature it’s ever seen, its voltage history, and total charge cycles,” Notaro said. “When the battery has finished its life in the car, the recyclers and integrators simply read the chip to determine the health of the cell, which allows them to sort it efficiently for either grid use or recycling.”

Bridges to adoption for legacy architectures

While chip-on-cell represents a move to smart cell architectures, Dukosi said DK-NFLNK is an upgrade path for manufacturers still using traditional module design. The system connects the node chip to the analog front ends via a serial interface, enabling wireless capability without changing the module hardware structure.

“DK-NFLNK and our full cell monitoring system are built on the same C-SynQ communication platform, giving battery manufacturers a real migration path,” Notaro concluded. “The engineers can upgrade their architecture today and move to full chip-on-cell monitoring in future product cycles.”

Dukosi’s monitoring technologies are now in commercial testing across several sectors. Nordic Marine Power has received DNV maritime approval for its PowerStack system using Dukosi monitoring, and Yichuan Intelligent Technology has incorporated the system into marine vessels in China.

As battery production scales globally, the industry is moving beyond pack manufacturing to long-term reliability and data.

data.title: Saskatchewan’s Semiconductor Strength Is Connecting the Pieces
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Canada’s geography makes covering its semiconductor industry something of a map-reading exercise. Expertise is spread across regional hubs, and the distance between complementary facilities makes collaboration a deliberate undertaking rather than something that happens over a casual lunch or networking event.

As Tyler Morhart, associate scientist and beamline lead at the Canadian Light Source’s (CLS’s) Synchrotron Laboratory for Micro and Nano Devices (SyLMAND), reminded EE Times in a recent conversation, this is an enormous country, with research infrastructure to match.

That makes Saskatchewan worth a closer look. The landlocked Prairie province has fewer than 1.3 million residents; its two largest cities are Saskatoon and the capital, Regina. The latter was recently selected for what could be one of Canada’s largest planned data center developments, to be built by Bell Canada, one of the country’s major telecommunications companies.

But the province has more to offer the rest of Canada than a convenient location for powerful AI servers: Saskatchewan is assembling a combination of computing infrastructure, quantum research, semiconductor design talent, and materials expertise that can strengthen both its own technology economy and the national semiconductor ecosystem.

The question isn’t whether Saskatchewan can do everything; it’s how well it can connect and scale up its existing strengths.

Compute meets real problems

More recently, Bell and Saskatchewan announced a non-binding agreement that creates a path to another 900 MW of AI infrastructure capacity, bringing the potential provincial total to 1.2 GW. Full development—including data centers, tenant computing equipment, and power generation—could represent more than C$50 billion (~$35 billion) in capital investment. Bell also plans to establish an AI Fabric head office in Saskatchewan.

It’s early days for this new initiative, but the initial 300-MW campus near Regina is more tangible, with more than 500 people working on the site and the first data hall targeted for the first half of 2027.

The expansion announcement follows the University of Saskatchewan’s (USask’s) acquisition of a full-stack quantum computer. The system includes a nine-qubit Rigetti Novera processor, which is modest beside the ambitions attached to Bell’s development, but the university’s case for owning it is refreshingly grounded: Researchers already have problems they want to investigate.

When EE Times spoke to Steven Rayan, director of USask’s Centre for Quantum Topology and Its Applications earlier this year, he described opportunities spanning vaccines, agriculture, energy, and secure communications. Researchers had already used quantum hardware in Quebec to investigate protein networks relevant to vaccine design and developed a quantum circuit to model northern microgrids combining solar generation and diesel power.

USask was also recently selected as a primary academic partner for the Canadian government’s Quantum Defence Innovation Secure Hub (DISH), hosted at the University of Calgary. The Bureau of Research, Engineering, and Advanced Leadership in Innovation and Science is establishing a national network of DISHes to provide secure, collaborative spaces for government, industry, academia, the Canadian Armed Forces, and national security partners to advance technologies that support defense and security applications.

Saskatchewan’s story isn’t confined to Saskatoon. Beyond Bell’s infrastructure investment, the University of Regina also conducts research in AI and machine learning.

Talent becomes a business

Computing capacity alone doesn’t make a semiconductor ecosystem. Someone still has to develop the tools and technologies behind it.

Siemens EDA’s Saskatoon operation illustrates the importance of sustained talent development. As Aaron Genest, technical director at Siemens EDA, explained when EE Times reported on Canada’s chip design capabilities, the operation’s growth has depended on university relationships, internal training, and an environment that encourages employees to stay. Experienced EDA specialists aren’t waiting on every street corner.

That university-to-industry pathway also supports entrepreneurship. Novigrad founders Christopher Elash and Lars Kishchuk met as USask engineering students and worked together on university space projects. Their early business ambitions were straightforward: Make chips.

Conversations with potential customers, however, helped redirect that enthusiasm toward another bottleneck: determining whether electronics can survive radiation exposure.

Novigrad’s founders describe an ecosystem with useful resources but not every capability. TRIUMF in British Columbia supplies radiation-testing infrastructure, while USask contributes expertise in semiconductor radiation effects.

Materials before machines

CLS adds another nearby resource that is critical for AI infrastructure but not talked about often enough: the materials underneath the hardware.

“Everything’s downstream of materials,” Morhart said. Conversations tend to jump directly from software to economic opportunity, but the hardware has to work.

An analytical chemist, Morhart runs the SyLMAND laboratory at CLS. He described CLS as “essentially a Swiss army knife,” with 22 beamlines adapted to different experiments. For semiconductor-related research, its contribution is advanced materials characterization, not conventional CMOS processing. The laboratory focuses on non-silicon microdevices and X-ray lithography.

Synchrotron techniques help researchers examine interfaces, transport, and degradation: not just what a material is but what happens when it becomes part of a working product. That makes CLS a national asset as well as a Saskatchewan advantage. It also illustrates the value of regional specialization. Alberta’s nanoFAB in Edmonton provides conventional semiconductor processing capabilities that Morhart’s group has deliberately chosen not to duplicate.

TRIUMF contributes a different capability through proton and neutron irradiation facilities used to investigate radiation effects on electronics. Characterization, fabrication, and radiation testing answer different questions; together, they create a broader development toolkit.

Making that toolkit accessible still takes effort. Morhart noted that connections across Canada require travel, professional networks, and deliberate relationship-building. Geographic separation doesn’t disappear because facilities are complementary. Organizations such as CMC Microsystems help bridge the distance with access to tools and experts.

Saskatchewan has the ingredients to scale up capabilities in AI, semiconductors, and quantum technologies in ways that complement those elsewhere in the country. What it needs to do is focus on making its own strengths easier to combine, commercialize, and connect nationally.

Bell’s infrastructure, USask’s quantum research, Siemens’s talent development, and Novigrad’s testing business are all good examples of how different parts of that challenge can be addressed.

Their value grows when companies and researchers can move between them—and reach beyond Saskatchewan when the next required capability lies elsewhere.

In a country as large and distributed as Canada, collaboration is a core component of any successful semiconductor strategy.

data.title: What It Takes to Let a Farm Robot Work Alone
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

For corn and soybean farmers in the U.S. Midwest, an autonomous machine could offer something more practical than replacing a worker: the ability to get more done with an already-lean team or spend less time in the field.

Salah Issa, associate professor in the Department of Agricultural and Biological Engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana–Champaign, sees both possibilities. He also pointed out that safety requirements for a large tractor differ from those of a small robot weeding vegetables or carrying produce alongside workers.

Agricultural autonomy encompasses machines with different weights, speeds, tasks, and operating environments. Before a farmer can leave one unsupervised, its manufacturer must establish which conditions allow that and how the machine will respond when those conditions change.

Different applications, different risks

Issa’s research focuses primarily on agricultural safety, with corn and soybean production forming much of his Midwest perspective. In those operations, he expects autonomy to help farmers expand capacity or improve working schedules.

“It’s more of the same operation, either doing it with a better life balance or over more acres to expand operations,” he told EE Times.

Fruit and vegetable production presents different opportunities. Tasks that currently require substantial manual labor can be automated, changing how workers and machines operate together. Issa describes produce-carrying robots that accompany workers and autonomous sprayers operating in orchards. The task and workflow determine where people encounter the equipment.

Across these applications, machines must cope with workers nearby, unexpected bystanders, animals, and changing outdoor conditions. The potential consequences of an encounter vary considerably between a small, slow platform and a large agricultural machine.

Different stopping distances and protective measures are needed for a small robot moving slowly between vegetable rows versus a large tractor. Issa said ISO 18497 provides a broad framework, but more detailed standards are needed for particular machines. The latest version points manufacturers toward additional obstacle-

detection guidance and leaves questions, such as how far from a person a machine should stop, open to be answered by application-specific guidelines.

Issa pointed to the use of a two-cylinder test object as a stand-in for a person when assessing obstacle detection. Other researchers have examined how well that approach translates to encounters with actual people. “They studied machines trained using the cylinders as stand-ins,” he said. “They found that when the machine operates with real humans, the level of accuracy drops.”

For Issa, reliable detection requires accounting for conditions in the field: “Vision systems get dusty. You’re dealing with vibrations, which impact the effectiveness and the longevity of sensors.” He therefore favors combining sensor types rather than depending on one technology.

The choice of safeguards, however, depends on the application. French robotics company Naïo illustrates an approach built around low speed, defined operating boundaries, and mechanical contact detection.

Designing for a defined operating area

Naïo offers two platforms: Oz, a small robot for vegetable growers and other specialist crops, and Ted, a robot that straddles vineyard rows, primarily for mechanical weeding. Matthias Carrière, Naïo’s managing director, is clear about his definition of autonomy. “When we talk about autonomy, we mean work without supervision,” he told EE Times.

Oz illustrates an approach built around a small, slow machine and a defined application. Its customers include vegetable farmers and seed producers, typically on farms of 1–20 hectares. The platform weighs about 150 kg, travels below 2 km/h, and works roughly half a hectare a day. Originally developed for weeding, it also supports sowing, planting, and transporting harvested produce.

Oz uses GPS with real-time kinematic positioning for guidance. A sensitive contact bumper triggers a stop when the machine encounters an obstruction. “A very light bump is enough, and it stops on contact,” Carrière said. He attributes that choice to Naïo’s assessment of the robot’s mass, speed, and intended operating conditions.

Contact-based protection necessarily acts after contact occurs. Its suitability therefore depends on the complete risk assessment, including the machine’s movement and task. Low speed alone does not establish that every possible encounter is harmless.

Naïo’s answer is not to make the perception system more sophisticated. “Our robots don’t use AI,” Carrière said. “We prioritize affordability and straightforward operation.”

The company’s approach extends beyond obstacle protection.

Carrière described a separate boundary-safety loop, with mapping distinct from that used to guide everyday work. “You must always isolate the loops,” he said. Following a route accurately and enforcing an approved operating boundary are separate functions.

Naïo also assesses individual parcels before approving unsupervised operation. Physical barriers can simplify containment; virtual boundaries are used elsewhere. Shared access routes and nearby activity can complicate the assessment.

“You can have all the AI and all the technology in the world,” Carrière said. “If the structure of a farm is not compatible with using a machine, and the farm is not ready to make structural changes, it won’t work.”

Protection can also interrupt useful work. On Ted, Naïo’s vineyard robot, vegetation growing beside a vine can trigger mechanical safeguards. Someone must investigate and clear the obstruction before unattended work resumes.

When people change the conditions

Repeated interruptions create a difficult engineering problem: Protection that gets in the way can encourage users to defeat it.

Issa recalled a demonstration where a manufacturer covered sensors with duct tape so a machine could operate with people nearby. His concern is that farmers, frustrated by frequent nuisance stops, could adopt the same workaround.

A safety mechanism can perform its intended function while prompting behavior that undermines it. Repeated alerts create a related problem: Users become accustomed to warnings and stop noticing them. Asking a person to intervene whenever the machine is uncertain has practical limits if the requests become burdensome.

“We’re now assuming the machines will respond to our interactions,” Issa said. “Then we change the way we interact based on how we assume the machine does.”

Manufacturers must consider how operating modes are communicated and how people may alter their behavior around the machine. The safety assessment also extends to setup, cleaning, maintenance, and other stages where workers remain involved.

Carrière said safety engineering must also anticipate what happens when users try to bypass the safeguards. Naïo prevents its robots from starting if required safety devices have been disabled. Even supervised operation is designed to make circumvention difficult: The operator must interact with the remote control every six minutes, confirming that someone remains near the machine. A farmer who deliberately rigs a way around such safeguards, Carrière said, crosses an important line: The manufacturer has designed for foreseeable misuse, but the user has intentionally defeated the safety system.

But responsibility cuts both ways. If Naïo determines that a robot can operate without anyone watching it, Carrière said the company assumes responsibility for that judgment: “It’s Naïo’s management that signs a document saying that, on this parcel, the robot can operate alone; on that parcel, it cannot—it must be supervised. That is how we assume responsibility.”

The approval relies partly on information supplied by the farmer, including whether an adjoining route is public or private. Users must respect the operating conditions. Carrière describes responsibilities for both parties, with Naïo standing behind its assessment and safety systems rather than assuming every possible liability.

But defining those responsibilities does not eliminate the unknowns that emerge once autonomous machines are operating in the field. Issa argued that learning from near-misses is therefore essential, particularly while deployment remains limited. Waiting for serious accidents would provide feedback too late. Unexpected encounters, confusing behavior, and situations that make users uncomfortable can reveal weaknesses earlier.

That emphasis on practical experience also helps explain Naïo’s priorities. Rather than continually adding technological sophistication, the company is focusing on simpler operation, additional useful tasks, and lower costs. “We’re not going to add innovation for innovation’s sake,” Carrière said. Working alone requires safeguards suited to the application—and evidence that they remain effective when people put the machine to work.

data.title: Can Jensen Keep His Job?
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Overnight, the multibillionaire rock star CEO of the world’s biggest technology company admitted to an affair with a Chinese intelligence asset, and no, this isn’t the plot of a sub-standard Bond movie. Can it really be true that someone with Jensen Huang’s intelligence, experience, and judgment got caught by a honey trap, possibly the oldest trick in the book when it comes to espionage?

Huang, 63, admitted an extramarital affair in a letter to Nvidia employees.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” he wrote in the letter. “You deserve better from me. Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.”

Rumors about Jensen Huang and Megaspeed executive Alice Huang (no relation) had been circulating for some time. Megaspeed is a Singaporean cloud provider and major Nvidia customer. U.S. intelligence believes Alice Huang is a Chinese asset, and is reportedly investigating whether Megaspeed may be illegally providing GPUs, AI compute, or both to restricted entities in China.

Jensen has been asked to appear at a closed-door briefing with the House Select Committee on Nov. 18. Nvidia’s board of directors is also beginning an independent investigation.

“The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” a statement from Nvidia’s board read.

While it’s unclear how much either U.S. intelligence or Nvidia’s board knew about this affair, and for how long, Nvidia spokespeople had previously appeared to deny the affair to the media, saying Jensen’s interactions with the Megaspeed executive were “not unusual or unexpected,” wording which, in retrospect, makes it sound like someone at Nvidia might have known. Nvidia’s board will now be checking everything the company has said is true to mitigate any legal ramifications.

It’s difficult to believe that someone with Jensen’s experience, and reported $200 billion fortune, underestimated the risks of an affair like this, whether he knew about his paramour’s connection to Chinese intelligence or not. Has the rock star CEO, one of the world’s richest men, known for his commanding leather-clad onstage performances, succumbed to his own hype?

Whether Jensen’s job outlasts this scandal or not, one thing that’s been irrevocably damaged is his public image. He has a cult-like following among tech bros, and is renowned for his charisma and his somewhat unconventional management style, famously keeping around 60 direct reports. Falling prey to a Chinese honey trap reveals a very human vulnerability that hardly fits his image. Fans were quick to defend him on social media both before and after the letter to employees emerged.

Another fan stepping up to publicly defend Jensen’s character was President Donald Trump.

“He’s such an honorable guy, I think he probably has an excuse for it,” Trump told reporters yesterday.

Asked by reporters whether Jensen should stay on as CEO of Nvidia, Trump replied, “Oh yeah, sure.”

The actual risk to U.S. national security seems debatable. While Jensen is an influential adviser to the Trump administration on AI policy, even being seated at the dinner table with Chinese President Xi Jinping on his state visit to the U.S. last month, Jensen himself has always lobbied for selling GPUs to China and is already a big supporter of open source AI models.

In footage filmed last month but released yesterday, Jensen tells Emily Chang that the Chinese “are not our enemies … If we care deeply about the safety of the world with respect to AI, then of course we must open dialogs, we must work with them in every possible way.”

So what would be the reason for targeting Jensen like this?

Could someone so influential be blackmailed with information like this, possibly in return for GPUs? Jensen’s own letter of admission seems to have put that to rest. Perhaps the destabilizing effect of a scandal of this magnitude would be a desirable outcome, though it remains to be seen how this will affect the market. Nvidia stock was slightly down yesterday, but not dramatically so, and something like this is unlikely to affect market demand for Nvidia’s products overall.

While it’s unclear how much U.S. intelligence or Nvidia’s board knew about this affair, it was the letter from the U.S. House Select Committee that brought it into the open. Why do this, and why now? Is someone trying to discredit Jensen as a major influence on the administration, or are they simply fed up with Nvidia skirting or flouting U.S. export controls? Trump is due to travel to China to meet with Xi later this month, and who knows whether Jensen will be invited.

If the CEO of the biggest technology company in the world, also the No. 1 supplier of AI chips with such huge geopolitical implications, is found to be a security risk of any kind, can he continue in his job? On the face of it, it may look like there’s no smoke without firing, but in the end it seems unlikely Nvidia’s investigation will find that the company or Jensen endangered national security, and most likely it will blow over. But given the strong link between Jensen’s public persona and Nvidia’s brand, can one continue to thrive without the other, and if so, is that a problem?

data.title: DeepX Tapes Out Second-Gen Chip, Projects 6.7× Performance Gain With LPDDR5x-PIM
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

South Korean edge AI chip startup DeepX has taped out its second-generation AI accelerator with access to custom processor-in-memory (PIM) technology from Samsung. The DX-M2 is designed to bring generative AI to robots, drones, and other edge devices, enabling inference of models with up to 100 billion parameters at less than 5 W.

DeepX’s first-generation chip, the DX-M1, is now in mass production, targeting vision applications. The newly taped-out DX-M2 aims to make local AI a practical choice for devices with tight power and thermal budgets. The chip is designed to run models with 20 billion to 100 billion parameters (approximately 3 billion to 20 billion active parameters) at 10 to 30 tokens per second, depending on the model. This is achieved within the same power budget as the M1—just 5 W.

“The most important change [between M1 and M2] is the memory bandwidth,” DeepX founder and CEO Lokwon Kim told EE Times.

Memory bandwidth has tripled from 50 to 150 GB/s, but there are several other efficiencies. DeepX said its NPU has doubled its power efficiency thanks to design improvements, and moving to a 2-nm process node doubled it again. 80 TOPS can now be achieved.

“This is important because with 5 W power consumption we can go everywhere, drones or any other battery-powered device,” Kim said. “Our goal is to enable deployment of sophisticated AI in all devices.”

The M2 can handle large mixture-of-experts LLMs and supports new techniques, including speculative decoding and TurboQuant.

Processor-in-memory

Most types of AI inference operations are constrained by moving weights between memory and compute, especially GEMV (general matrix-vector multiplication), during which random memory accesses are required, slowing down computation. Memory makers have come up with PIM schemes in which memory-bound operations such as GEMV can be computed inside the memory chip. Doing operations within memory increases the effective memory bandwidth and reduces time-consuming memory access times.

PIM is set to become a JEDEC standard for LPDDR6. However, DeepX has been working with Samsung on integrating the DX-M2 with Samsung’s LPDDR5x-PIM.

“We have spent one and a half years on this technology, collaborating with Samsung Memory, as they already have their custom PIM for LPDDR5x,” Kim said. “We already received LPDDR5x PIM samples and we are testing the operations and performance in-house.”

DeepX’s simulations show that offloading GEMV operations from the DX-M2 into LPDDR5x-PIM will result in 6.7× the tokens per second for Llama3.1-8B versus the DX-M2 alone.

“DX-M2 with LPDDR5x-PIM is close to optimal,” Kim said. “But our next generation, the DX-M3, will support official LPDDR6 PIM technology; then we can get the full theoretical performance advancement, which is 5× to 8× higher performance.”

The only drawback, Kim explained, is that the extra compute doesn’t come for free—6.7× the performance needs 2.7× the power consumption overall. That said, DeepX thinks it can get a 2× performance uplift within the same power envelope as non-PIM operation.

“Substantial manual effort” is required in the compiler to support this mode of operation, Kim said, noting DeepX currently has a prototype compiler running, based on a simulation of the PIM-enabled LPDDR5x. “We are now making the hardware modules so that we can test that in the physical environment, so we couldn’t finish the compiler yet, but we are actively working on it.”

Key markets

The DX-M2 will target several key sectors. DeepX is working with Taiwanese OEMs to find the right sweet spot for AI PCs, including laptops and workstations. Robotics companies, currently prototyping on GPUs such as Nvidia Thor, want lower power and more compute on-device, and automotive companies are looking for a low-power chip that can run agents in-vehicle, Tim Park, director of strategic marketing at DeepX, told EE Times. For IoT devices, DeepX is already working with Samsung on a next-generation smart hub. The company is also joining the AWS IoT ecosystem so it can use Greengrass to support remote model updates.

Robotics customers typically begin development on GPUs but have to look for alternatives due to thermal and power consumption considerations, Park said. DeepX is working hard to enable transitions from the Nvidia Isaac robotics platform to its in-house equivalent, Newton.

“Robotics customers ask us about our hardware, but also about how they can migrate from Nvidia to DeepX,” he said. “This is the answer—customers change their APIs to call Newton instead of Isaac and then they can run the exact same pipeline on the DeepX system.”

DeepX has 17 compatible libraries up and running, Park said. The company has demonstrated M1-based robots using the same source code as an Nvidia Jetson-based robot, but calling the DeepX libraries.

“The actual outcome for the customer is they can enjoy 20 times longer battery life and [lower cost] when they switch from Nvidia to DeepX,” Kim said. “At the same time, the switching time can be under a second. They just need to change the API name from Isaac to Newton. That’s it.”

A full robotics stack for DeepX hardware is currently under development.

DeepX is engaging with robotics customers in the U.S., China, Vietnam, and Korea, while Hyundai Motor Group Robotics Lab is already using the DX-M1 in its robotics platform.

Meanwhile, the company is building out its ecosystem, adding Taiwanese OEMs, vertical champions in various markets and, lately, a collaboration with Intel.

DeepX is working with Intel to integrate OpenVINO with the DeepX SDK in order to tap into Intel’s x86 customer base. The DX-M1 can complement integrated NPUs in Intel Core Ultra CPUs and enable AI for other Intel edge CPUs that don’t have an NPU, offloading some or all of the AI workload.

The company recently met with AMD to discuss jointly developing a robotics platform based on DeepX accelerators combined with AMD’s Kria reference board, in particular for the Korean ecosystem, Kim said. This is part of DeepX’s drive to collaborate with other heterogeneous ecosystems, including Raspberry Pi and Baidu’s PaddlePaddle ecosystem.

Commercial traction

DeepX has more than 100 purchase orders for the DX-M1 so far, from all major global markets across all physical AI industries (including drones, robots, smart factory, surveillance camera, aerospace and defense, healthcare, and IoT), Kim said. The M1 is now in mass production.

The most active market for physical AI was previously China, Kim said, but Japan has emerged this year as a major market, with a strong willingness to pioneer humanoid robots.

“All the large Japanese companies are evaluating our chips, more than 10 leading companies in Japan right now, and their feedback is very encouraging,” he said. “At the same time, the U.S. market [is strong]; we have several big names there, and their feedback is really good.”

DeepX is also engaged in smart city projects in South Korea, Vietnam, and Singapore.

“Our long-term view is that AI compute will become more distributed as efficiency improves,” Park said. “The PC and smartphone eras showed how computing can spread into many products. AI will follow its own path, but local inference has clear value when an application needs immediate access to sensor data or operation without continuous connectivity.”

DeepX considers edge AI to be a substantial opportunity for its chips, Park said, especially at a time when the amount of power available for new data centers is limited.

Kim’s belief is that just as only a quarter of the CPU market is in the data center today, the AI processor market will also shift to the edge in the next five to 10 years.

At a time when many AI data center projects are delayed, the AI capacity issue can’t be solved with investment alone, he added. AI chips that consume just 5 W can enable migration of AI to the device.

“If we deploy models up to 100 billion parameters in devices, we can reduce AI data center traffic by more than 80%,” Kim said. “That means we could have five times larger infrastructure without adding any AI servers. This is our vision.”

On the roadmap for DeepX’s third generation is the DX-M3, coming in 2028. The M3 will be chiplet-based and will target 1 ePOPS (INT8) using LPDDR6-PIM. The main target markets for this are automotive OEMs and humanoid robotics companies, whose demands will require multi-chiplet designs.

In the meantime, samples of the M2 are expected in March 2027, with mass production targeted for fall 2027.
